title: SkillSmith: Enhancing Locally Deployed Agents via Automatic Skill Construction and Evolution
prompt:
I've been brainstorming a way to bootstrap high-quality Skills for a Local Agent without relying on expert-authored initialization. The core idea is Skill Creation: rather than naively asking the Cloud Agent to directly write a Skill from a task description (which is unreliable since the Cloud Agent isn't initially familiar with the target application scenario and may invent unsupported rules or miss implicit procedures), the approach is inspired by how human experts learn a new application scenario — by trying tasks, checking outcomes, reflecting, and summarizing reusable insights into Skills. Based on this, I'm designing an agentic Skill Creation pipeline consisting of two steps to produce a high-quality initial Skill $\mathcal{S}_0$.

My setup: the offline Cloud Agent is implemented with the Claude Code SDK using Claude Opus 4.7 as the backbone model, and the Local Agent is implemented with the Hermes agent framework using Qwen3.6-27B as the backbone model. Skill Evolution runs for five rounds, with $L_{\max}=400$ lines for the main manual and each reference file capped at 250 lines. For fair comparison, all non-cloud methods are evaluated with the same Hermes agent framework and Qwen3.6-27B backbone. This particular comparison isolates the offline Skill Creation stage before any Skill Evolution is applied, using the SkillSmith framework.

My baseline results, without any Skill (No Skill condition), are: AppWorld-Normal PR (Pass Rate) = 36.3%, AppWorld-Challenge PR = 28.1%, and WorkBench PR = 51.1%.

My question about this setup: after switching from No Skill (my baseline above) to Skill Creation only, predict the resulting value for each: AppWorld-Normal PR (Pass Rate %) (in %); AppWorld-Challenge PR (Pass Rate %) (in %); WorkBench PR (Pass Rate %) (in %).

title: SkillSmith: Enhancing Locally Deployed Agents via Automatic Skill Construction and Evolution
prompt:
I've been brainstorming ways to close the gap between the initial Skill produced by the Skill Creation stage and what my frozen Local Agent actually needs. The issue is that Skill Creation gives me an initial Skill $\mathcal{S}_0$, but this Skill is distilled mainly from Cloud Agent executions and may not fully match the failure modes of the frozen Local Agent. Some knowledge may be missing, some references may not be loaded under the right conditions, and some instructions may be too weak for the Local Agent to follow reliably. So the idea is a Skill Evolution stage that iteratively improves the current Skill $\mathcal{S}_{i-1}$ using Local Agent failures, evaluator feedback, and Cloud Agent analysis, where each evolution iteration consists of two steps.

My setup: I implement the Local Agent based on the Hermes agent framework using Qwen3.6-27B as the backbone model, within SkillSmith. Skill Evolution runs for at five rounds, applied right after the Skill Creation stage completes.

As my current baseline, with Skill Creation only (before Skill Evolution is applied), I get: AppWorld-Normal PR (Pass Rate %) = 66.3%, AppWorld-Challenge PR (Pass Rate %) = 71.6%, and WorkBench PR (Pass Rate %) = 87.8%.

My question about this setup: after switching from Skill Creation only (my baseline above) to Creation + Evolution, predict the resulting value for each: AppWorld-Normal PR (Pass Rate %) (in %); AppWorld-Challenge PR (Pass Rate %) (in %); WorkBench PR (Pass Rate %) (in %).

title: SkillSmith: Enhancing Locally Deployed Agents via Automatic Skill Construction and Evolution

I've been brainstorming an approach where a Skill is built offline through Cloud Agent exploration and evolution, and then loaded into a frozen Local Agent for evaluation, and I want to compare this against Doc-Prompting, which injects API-level tool documentation and operation manuals into the prompt as its way of giving the agent environment knowledge.

My setup: the offline Cloud Agent is implemented with the Claude Code SDK using Claude Opus 4.7 as the backbone model, and the Local Agent is implemented based on the Hermes agent framework using Qwen3.6-27B (SLM) as the backbone model. Skill Evolution runs for at five rounds. I set $L_{\max}=400$ lines for the main manual and cap each reference file at 250 lines. For a fair comparison, all non-cloud methods, including Doc-Prompting, are evaluated with the same Hermes agent framework and Qwen3.6-27B backbone model. The overall structure is that an Offline Learning Phase constructs and evolves a target-scenario Skill from representative tasks and evaluator feedback through Cloud-Local Agent collaboration, and then the Online Serving Phase deploys the frozen Local Agent with the produced Skill, with no Cloud LLM calls and all user data kept local.

My baseline results for Doc-Prompting under this setup are: on AppWorld-Normal, Pass Rate (PR) = 28.0% and Average evaluator Score (AS) = 0.508 score; on AppWorld-Challenge, Pass Rate (PR) = 21.6% and Average evaluator Score (AS) = 0.451 score; and on WorkBench, Pass Rate (PR) = 47.4%.

title: SkillSmith: Enhancing Locally Deployed Agents via Automatic Skill Construction and Evolution
prompt:
I've been brainstorming ways to compare a Skill-based approach against memory-based methods like ExpeL for improving agent performance without touching model parameters. ExpeL works by extracting natural-language insights and compact successful trajectories from agent trajectories and retrieving relevant memories during task execution. The idea I'm working with instead builds a Skill artifact offline via a Cloud Agent that explores tasks and evolves the skill over multiple rounds, and this Skill is then loaded into a separate Local Agent for evaluation, rather than relying on retrieved memory snippets at inference time.

My setup: the offline Cloud Agent is implemented with the Claude Code SDK, using Claude Opus 4.7 as the backbone model, and it's this Cloud Agent that performs the exploration and evolution of the Skill. The Local Agent, which is what actually gets evaluated, is built on the Hermes agent framework using a frozen Qwen3.6-27B (SLM) backbone. Skill Evolution runs for five rounds. I cap the main manual at $L_{\max}=400$ lines, and each reference file is capped at 250 lines. For fair comparison, all non-cloud methods, including ExpeL, are evaluated using this same Hermes agent framework and the same Qwen3.6-27B backbone model.

My baseline results with ExpeL under this setup are: on AppWorld-Normal, PR = 65.9% and AS = 0.816; on AppWorld-Challenge, PR = 62.1% and AS = 0.867; and on WorkBench, PR = 49.5%.

My question about this setup: after switching from ExpeL (my baseline above) to SkillSmith (ours), predict the resulting value for each: AppWorld-Normal PR (in %); AppWorld-Normal AS; AppWorld-Challenge PR (in %); AppWorld-Challenge AS; WorkBench PR (in %).

title: SkillSmith: Enhancing Locally Deployed Agents via Automatic Skill Construction and Evolution
prompt:
I've been brainstorming around a notion of an Agent Skill, formalized as S=(M,R,C), where M is the main Markdown file SKILL.md (the main manual) containing metadata, general instructions, and pointers to references in R; R={r_j}_{j=1}^{J} stores reference files with environment rules and operation procedures, and C={κ_j}_{j=1}^{J} records the loading condition for each reference. The idea is that Skills support progressive disclosure: during execution, the Agent first reads the general guidance in M and only loads a reference file r_j ∈ R when its loading condition κ_j ∈ C is satisfied, which is meant to make Skills context-efficient.

The overall setup I'm working with splits into an Offline Learning Phase, which constructs and evolves a target-scenario Skill from representative tasks and evaluator feedback through Cloud-Local Agent collaboration, and an Online Serving Phase, which deploys the frozen Local Agent with the produced Skill, with no Cloud LLM calls and all user data kept local.

Concretely, my Local Agent is implemented using the Hermes agent framework with Qwen3.6-27B as the backbone model. Skill Evolution runs for five rounds. I set L_max=400 lines for the main manual and cap each reference file at 250 lines. For a fair comparison, all non-cloud methods are evaluated with the same Hermes agent framework and Qwen3.6-27B backbone model, and the Cloud-agent baselines also use the Hermes agent framework but replace the local backbone with the corresponding cloud LLM.

Right now, for the vanilla Local Agent setting (Qwen3.6-27B, Vanilla with frontier SLMs, no Skill loaded), my baseline results are: on AppWorld-Normal, PR = 36.3% and AS = 0.525 score; on AppWorld-Challenge, PR = 28.1% and AS = 0.424 score; and on WorkBench, PR = 51.1%.

My question about this setup: after switching from Qwen3.6-27B (Vanilla with frontier SLMs) (my baseline above) to SkillSmith (ours), predict the resulting value for each: AppWorld-Normal PR (in %); AppWorld-Normal AS (in score); AppWorld-Challenge PR (in %); AppWorld-Challenge AS (in score); WorkBench PR (in %).

title: Privacy-Preserving Data Drift Detection and Recovery for Large-Scale LLM Applications via Proxy Representations
prompt:
I've been brainstorming how to improve synthetic proxy generation for ProxyDrift, specifically comparing a basic independent sampler against a conditional (Chow-Liu) sampler. The motivation is that a basic independence sampler treats each dimension independently, drawing from per-dimension marginals, which discards all correlations and routinely produces implausible combinations (e.g., a Legal Document output type paired with a Casual tone) -- artefacts that exercise the model on inputs no real user would issue, biasing quality estimates and wasting evaluation budget. So the idea is to use a sampler that respects the joint structure of the dimensions instead.

The approach models the joint distribution over $D$ dimensions using the Chow-Liu optimal tree approximation: the maximum-weight spanning tree over dimensions with mutual information as edge weights. For every dimension pair $(X_i, X_j)$, with vocabularies $\mathcal{V}_i$ and $\mathcal{V}_i$, I maintain a contingency table of co-occurrence counts from raw proxy records. For multi-valued dimensions, every combination of values from the two dimensions in the same record contributes a count. Joint-derived marginals ensure consistency:
\begin{equation}
 p(v_i) = \sum_{v_j} p(v_i, v_j), \quad
 \MI(X_i; X_j) = \sum_{v_i, v_j} p(v_i, v_j)
 \ln \frac{p(v_i, v_j)}{p(v_i)\,p(v_j)}
\end{equation}
The Chow-Liu theorem states that the optimal tree-structured approximation is the maximum-weight spanning tree with MI as edge weights. I construct it via Kruskal's algorithm with union-find (rank compression and path halving), yielding $O(D^2 \log D)$ complexity.

My setup tests whether the full pipeline can produce a synthetic dataset whose proxy distribution matches production. I use the redundancy-aware (RA) alignment score, and report results for the Excel document-generation scenario, since results for other document types (e.g., PowerPoint) are almost identical. This evaluation predates the taxonomy-refinement loop -- it's evaluated against the unrefined (pre-refinement) proxy taxonomy, to see whether distribution-aware sampling is worth pursuing in the first place.

Reference distributions were computed from a week of production traffic (2026-04-02 to 2026-04-08). Two samplers each produced a synthetic dataset of ~1,000 proxies: the basic (dimensionally independent) sampler, drawing each dimension from its production marginal, and the conditional (Chow-Liu) sampler described above. As a third point of reference, I also plan to re-score the pre-existing hand-curated Excel test set against the same production baseline.

My current baseline result: for the Excel document generation scenario, on production traffic from 2026-04-02 to 2026-04-08, the basic (independent) sampler gets an RA alignment score of 0.897.

My question about this setup: after switching from Basic (independent) sampler (my baseline above) to Conditional (Chow-Liu) sampler, predict the resulting value for each: Excel document generation scenario production traffic (2026-04-02 to 2026-04-08) RA alignment score (in RA score).

title: TRACE-Memory: Public-Conditioned Retrieval and Utility-Aware Evidence Admission for Personalized Generation
prompt:
I've been mulling over how to handle the fact that a memory's incremental value can't really be scored before retrieval, since that value depends jointly on the task and on what the public context already provides. The idea I keep coming back to is splitting the process into two stages: a Stage 1 query policy that predicts the user-specific information missing from the public context $p$ and expresses these gaps as retrieval queries (turning unobserved value estimation into coverage-oriented retrieval), and a Stage 2 policy that takes the coverage-oriented candidate pool and converts it into a precision-oriented evidence set by evaluating incremental utility.

Concretely, Stage 1 uses a query policy $\pi_{\phi}$ to generate a canonical list of public-conditioned information gaps, $Z=(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_L)$, $Z\sim\pi_\phi(\cdot\mid q,p)$, $L\leq L_{\max}$, where each $z_i$ describes a missing user preference, reaction, tolerance, or behavioral pattern rather than repeating public facts about the target item. The retriever then executes these queries over personal history and aggregates results under a shared budget: $C_{\mathrm{mem}}=\mathcal{R}(Z,\mathcal{M}_u)=\operatorname{Aggregate}\!\left(\bigcup_{z_i\in Z}\operatorname{Retrieve}(z_i,\mathcal{M}_u)\right)$, using BGE-base-en-v1.5 embeddings. Stage 1 is deliberately recall-oriented, maximizing the opportunity to recover useful personal information but leaving admission to Stage 2.

Stage 2 evaluates the coverage-oriented pool, which may be redundant, weakly supported, or already covered by public context. $\Psi$ produces fine-grained evidence units $C_{\mathrm{evi}}=\Psi(C_{\mathrm{mem}})=\{e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_K\}$, each retaining its source identifier, offsets, and timestamp for attributability. Stage 2 outputs an action $A=(\langle id_1,a_1\rangle,\ldots,\langle id_J,a_J\rangle,\texttt{STOP})\sim\pi_\omega(\cdot\mid q,p,Z,C_{\mathrm{evi}})$, $S(A)\subseteq C_{\mathrm{evi}}$, with $a_j$ an extractive anchor, conditioning on $Z$ to preserve the information-gap intent, and $\texttt{EMPTY}$ mapping to $S(A)=\varnothing$.

The core of what I'm testing is the incremental utility formulation: since $U_u$ is unavailable, I measure how the selected evidence $S$ changes the frozen generator's distribution along a target response $y^*$ relative to the public-only path, with the target used only for offline rewards, never as input to either policy or the retriever. At position $t$, $p_t^S=p_G(\cdot\mid y_{<t}^*,q,p,\Gamma(S))$ and $p_t^\varnothing=p_G(\cdot\mid y_{<t}^*,q,p)$, and I use per-token likelihood gain and entropy reduction: $\Delta L(S)=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[\log p_t^S(y_t^*)-\log p_t^\varnothing(y_t^*)\right]$ and $\Delta H(S)=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[H(p_t^\varnothing)-H(p_t^S)\right]$, where positive $\Delta L(S)$ means the evidence better explains the observed response and positive $\Delta H(S)$ means it reduces uncertainty along that path. The evidence reward combines these with compactness and validity constraints: $R_E(A)=\Delta L(S(A))+\eta\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[\Delta L(S(A))\geq-\epsilon_L\right]\Delta H(S(A))-\lambda_E\operatorname{Cost}_E(S(A))-\lambda_V\mathbf{1}\!\left[\operatorname{Invalid}(A)\right]$, with $\operatorname{Cost}_E(S)=\alpha_E|S|+\beta_E\operatorname{Len}(\Gamma(S))$. Invalid actions include malformed outputs, unavailable evidence identifiers, and ID-anchor inconsistencies, and since $\Gamma(\varnothing)=\epsilon$, $R_E(\texttt{EMPTY})=0$.

My setup is TRACE-Memory trained on 4,500 tasks: 2,500 rule-generated Goodreads Controlled tasks instantiated from predefined task types and book metadata, and 2,000 Natural tasks from Goodreads, Amazon Reviews, and Reddit (1,000/500/500). Validation and test each add 450 tasks in the same source proportions, for 5,400 total, each including a request, public context, target-user history, and reference response, with target-item interactions excluded from memory. Stage 1 uses Qwen3-1.7B or Qwen3-4B; Stage 2 uses Qwen3-4B or Llama-3.2-3B; both use LoRA. The BGE-base-en-v1.5 retriever, segmenter, and generator remain frozen, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash constructs SFT targets. Training uses structured SFT, reduced-space stage-wise GRPO, and nested multi-sample Joint GRPO, where Stage 1 samples multiple query lists and Stage 2 samples multiple evidence actions under each query-induced candidate pool, with each Stage 2 action receiving direct evidence utility and the mean utility within its action group defining the reward of the corresponding Stage 1 query. I'm comparing against a Public-only baseline (no evidence at all), among other baselines, keeping generation settings and evidence budgets shared across comparisons. I'm using frozen response generators DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, or GPT-5.4, and I evaluate with the signed preference advantage metric, $\operatorname{Adv}(A,B)=\Pr(A\succ B)-\Pr(B\succ A)$, where positive values favor $A$, comparing TRACE-Memory's evidence selection against the Public-only baseline on both the Controlled (Goodreads) and Natural (Goodreads, Amazon Reviews, Reddit) task settings, with the generator fixed and only memory querying and selection differing between methods.

title: TRACE-Memory: Public-Conditioned Retrieval and Utility-Aware Evidence Admission for Personalized Generation
prompt:
I've been working on a two-stage approach to memory-augmented response generation where the first stage builds a coverage-oriented pool of candidate memories, and the second stage is meant to convert that pool into a precision-oriented set by evaluating the incremental utility of the evidence that would actually reach the generator. The concern motivating stage 2 is that the coverage-oriented pool from stage 1 may contain redundant, weakly supported, or publicly covered memories.

In this setup, a module Ψ produces fine-grained evidence units from the memory pool: $C_{\mathrm{evi}} = \Psi(C_{\mathrm{mem}}) = \{e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_K\}$, where each unit keeps its source identifier, offsets, and timestamp so selected evidence stays attributable to its original interaction. Stage 2 then samples an action sequence $A = (\langle id_1,a_1\rangle,\ldots,\langle id_J,a_J\rangle,\texttt{STOP}) \sim \pi_\omega(\cdot\mid q,p,Z,C_{\mathrm{evi}})$, with $S(A)\subseteq C_{\mathrm{evi}}$ and each $a_j$ an extractive anchor. Conditioning on $Z$ preserves the information-gap intent from stage 1, and an $\texttt{EMPTY}$ action maps to $S(A)=\varnothing$.

To evaluate incremental utility, since a ground-truth utility signal $U_u$ is unavailable, I measure how the selected evidence $S$ changes the frozen generator's distribution along a target response $y^*$ relative to the public-only path (the target is used only for offline rewards, never as input to either the policy or the retriever). At position $t$, I define $p_t^S = p_G(\cdot\mid y_{<t}^*,q,p,\Gamma(S))$ and $p_t^\varnothing = p_G(\cdot\mid y_{<t}^*,q,p)$, then compute per-token likelihood gain $\Delta L(S) = T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[\log p_t^S(y_t^*)-\log p_t^\varnothing(y_t^*)\right]$ and entropy reduction $\Delta H(S) = T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left[H(p_t^\varnothing)-H(p_t^S)\right]$. Positive $\Delta L(S)$ means the evidence better explains the observed response; positive $\Delta H(S)$ means it reduces uncertainty along that path.

The evidence reward combines these signals with compactness and validity constraints: $R_E(A) = \Delta L(S(A)) + \eta\,\mathbf{1}[\Delta L(S(A))\geq-\epsilon_L]\Delta H(S(A)) - \lambda_E\operatorname{Cost}_E(S(A)) - \lambda_V\mathbf{1}[\operatorname{Invalid}(A)]$, with $\operatorname{Cost}_E(S) = \alpha_E|S|+\beta_E\operatorname{Len}(\Gamma(S))$. Invalid actions include malformed outputs, unavailable evidence identifiers, and ID-anchor inconsistencies, and $\Gamma(\varnothing)=\epsilon$.

My setup compares this trained selection policy against baselines that share the same inputs, evidence budgets, and generation settings, differing only in memory querying and selection: Public-only (no evidence), Random (random history), and All (the full pool injected without selection). The generator is frozen — I'm testing with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, or GPT-5.4 — paired with TRACE-Memory trained policies as described above. I report signed preference advantage, $\operatorname{Adv}(A,B) = \Pr(A\succ B)-\Pr(B\succ A)$, where positive values favor $A$.

title: ForestBench: A Unified Graph Framework for Evaluating Multi-Agent Collaboration
prompt:

title: Physics-Informed Learning for Robust Acoustic Localization with Calibrated Uncertainty
prompt:
I've been developing an approach to physics-plausibility gating with a learned correction on top of a hyperbolic solver, aimed at bounding the catastrophic tail of localization errors without disturbing the cases where the solver is already reliable. The idea is to keep a TabPFN regression model that predicts source $x$ and $y$ coordinates independently, using 72 physics-informed tabular features per detection, with the hyperbolic solver's own position estimate included as one of the input features so the learned model is refining the physics-based solution rather than localizing from scratch. By default I retain the solver's estimate, and I only substitute the TabPFN prediction on detections flagged as unreliable by a two-stage plausibility gate. The first stage checks whether the solver's estimate falls within a bounding box around the microphone array, expanded outward by a tunable margin proportional to the array's spatial extent; anything outside is rejected unconditionally. The second stage, applied only to estimates surviving the first, computes an energy-consistency score as the RMS residual between each microphone pair's observed log-amplitude ratio and the ratio predicted from the candidate position under $1/r$ spherical spreading, and flags the estimate if this residual exceeds a threshold $\tau^*$. Since source loudness and microphone sensitivity cancel in the ratio, this check needs no absolute sound-level calibration; it's the amplitude-domain analogue of ratio-based energy localization, used here as a plausibility check rather than as a localizer itself. I select $\tau^*$ on simulation data alone, choosing the most permissive value by grid search that achieves at least a threefold improvement in 99th-percentile error for no more than a 20% increase in median error relative to the unsubstituted solver, then apply it unchanged to the field data with no tuning on field labels. A detection gets substituted with the TabPFN prediction if either the geometric check fails or the energy-consistency residual exceeds $\tau^*$; otherwise the solver's estimate is kept. My setup uses simulated multichannel acoustic experiments generated with the ForestIR package for the frozen-lake site, a low-noise, treeless site (so trunk scattering is disabled in simulation), with a bird-vocalization source placed at random 2D locations relative to a fixed three-microphone array in an approximately equilateral geometry with roughly 50 m inter-microphone spacing, microphones and speakers at 1.2 m height. Simulated weather is sampled from the range recorded during the real experiment (-19 to -6 degrees C, 70-95% RH), and each simulated recording draws one noise regime at random from the site's own recorded background, synthetic white, or pink noise, each at a fixed level. I also have real playback recordings from the Konnevesi Research Station field experiment (February 24, 2026) at this same site, covering four settings (two with a 16-species European stimulus set, two with a 30-species North American set) from six known speaker positions, one with a known hardware failure, with playback streams synchronized via PPS timing to about 1 cm in propagation distance and segmented into single-signal clips of 2.18-11.00 s (mean 5.07 s). Given TabPFN's in-context conditioning rather than training on all available data, I use an approximately 90/10 train-test split with the training set capped at 1,000 examples. I'm following the field-evaluation protocol: the model is trained on simulation only and evaluated on the real field recordings, with every field position withheld entirely from training, as well as evaluating on held-out simulation positions. My baseline, using just the hyperbolic solver's output (the point-estimate model input feature) before any gating or correction, gets the following on the frozen-lake site: on real playback recordings (Konnevesi), mean = 5.13 m, p50 = 0.41 m, p90 = 24.6 m, p95 = 42.1 m, p99 = 43.7 m; on simulation, mean = 0.17 m, p50 = 0.04 m, p90 = 0.21 m, p95 = 0.36 m, p99 = 3.88 m.

title: Triple Expert Learning from Noisy Labels for Semi-Supervised Vision Foundation Model Adaptation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming a way to make semi-supervised adaptation of a frozen vision foundation model more robust to pseudo-label noise. The idea, which I'm calling TriNoL (triple LoRA expert routing), is motivated by the observation that pseudo-labels in SSL are not equally reliable: high-confidence pseudo-labels usually give useful supervision, low-confidence ones are often noisy or misleading, and medium-confidence ones sit in an ambiguous region where the model hasn't formed a stable decision boundary yet. Standard PEFT-based SSL methods typically funnel all pseudo-label gradients through a single LoRA adapter, which can be fragile since a small LoRA update space is easily disrupted by unreliable pseudo-labels.

My setup replaces that single adapter with three confidence-aware expert branches, all implemented as lightweight LoRA modules while the VFM backbone stays frozen. The expert set is \(\mathcal{E}=\{e^{+},e^{a},e^{-}\}\): the Positive Expert $e^{+}$ learns from high-confidence pseudo-labels and captures reliable adaptation directions; the Negative Expert $e^{-}$ handles low-confidence pseudo-labels to reduce the harmful effect of unreliable supervision; and the Alignment Expert $e^{a}$ focuses on medium-confidence pseudo-labels to improve alignment of ambiguous samples near class boundaries. I use a pretrained vision foundation model as the visual encoder, with backbone parameters $\psi$ kept frozen, and a LoRA module inserted into selected linear projections. The trainable parameters are the LoRA experts plus a classifier head $C_{\omega}$ with parameters $\omega$.

For a frozen linear projection with weight $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}$, each expert $e$ learns an independent low-rank update \(\Delta W^{e}=B^{e}A^{e}\), where $A^{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}$ and $B^{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r}$ are trainable matrices and $r$ is the LoRA rank. The adapted projection for expert $e$ is \(h^{e}=Wx+\alpha\Delta W^{e}x\), where $x$ is the input feature and $\alpha$ is the LoRA scaling factor. $W$ is shared across all experts, while $\Delta W^{+}$, $\Delta W^{a}$, and $\Delta W^{-}$ are expert-specific.

During training, I use the weakly augmented unlabeled view to estimate pseudo-label confidence, with the Positive Expert (trained on labeled data and high-confidence unlabeled samples) producing the pseudo-labels by default: \(p_i^w=\operatorname{softmax}\big(z^{+}(u_i^w)\big)\), where $z^{+}(u_i^w)$ are its logits. The pseudo-label and confidence are \(\hat{y}_i=\arg\max_{c} p_{i,c}^w\), \(q_i=\max_{c} p_{i,c}^w\). I use two confidence thresholds $\tau_{+}$ and $\tau_{-}$ with $0 \leq \tau_{-}<\tau_{+}\leq 1$, splitting unlabeled samples into three regions: \(\mathcal{B}_{u}^{+} = \{u_i \in \mathcal{B}_u \mid q_i \geq \tau_{+}\}\), \(\mathcal{B}_{u}^{a} = \{u_i \in \mathcal{B}_u \mid \tau_{-} \leq q_i < \tau_{+}\}\), \(\mathcal{B}_{u}^{-} = \{u_i \in \mathcal{B}_u \mid q_i < \tau_{-}\}\). Samples in $\mathcal{B}_{u}^{+}$ go to the Positive Expert, $\mathcal{B}_{u}^{a}$ to the Alignment Expert, and $\mathcal{B}_{u}^{-}$ to the Negative Expert, using the same confidence signal already present in standard SSL pipelines without an extra routing network. Labeled samples are used throughout to maintain stable supervised learning and anchor the adaptation to ground-truth supervision.

All methods, including mine, are evaluated under the same semi-supervised VFM adaptation setting with a frozen backbone and trainable LoRA-based adaptation modules, across varying numbers of labeled samples per class and varying labeled/unlabeled data ratios, on CIFAR-100, FOOD-101, Semi-Aves, and ImageNet.

My current baseline results (from prior SSL/VFM adaptation baselines: Labeled Only, PL, FixMatch, FlexMatch, FreeMatch, SoftMatch, DebiasPL, V-PET, FineSSL) are as follows. On CIFAR-100: N4/N25/N100 accuracy for Labeled Only is 64.36%/80.44%/84.62%; for PL is 66.35%/81.64%/84.84%; for FixMatch is 77.31%/84.23%/86.35%; for FlexMatch is 79.39%/83.96%/86.42%; for FreeMatch is 76.39%/83.8%/86.53%; for SoftMatch is 76.15%/84.04%/86.49%; for DebiasPL is 79.78%/84.22%/86.35%; for V-PET is 80.52%/84.65%/86.88%; for FineSSL is 80.66%/84.72%/86.86%.

On FOOD-101: N2/N4/N10 accuracy for Labeled Only is 61.64%/73.92%/82.29%; for PL is 58.43%/77.78%/84.81%; for FixMatch is 75.13%/85.12%/88.91%; for FlexMatch is 81.18%/88.72%/89.43%; for FreeMatch is 74.54%/84.89%/89.15%; for SoftMatch is 76.04%/85.26%/89.2%; for DebiasPL is 86.73%/88.82%/89.52%; for V-PET is 87.58%/89.74%/90.05%; for FineSSL is 87.27%/89.49%/89.88%.

On Semi-Aves, D_in / D_in+D_out accuracy for FixMatch is 65.76%/60.46%; for FlexMatch is 64.88%/58.38%; for FreeMatch is 64.78%/58.35%; for SoftMatch is 65.08%/58.24%; for DebiasPL is 67.11%/61.07%; for FineSSL is 67.51%/61.3%.

On ImageNet, 1% / 10% accuracy for FixMatch is 73.41%/78.95%; for FlexMatch is 73.4%/78.98%; for FreeMatch is 73.1%/78.75%; for SoftMatch is 73.17%/78.79%; for DebiasPL is 73.89%/79.01%; for FineSSL is 74.46%/79.42%.

My question about this setup: after switching from Prior SSL/VFM adaptation baselines (Labeled Only, PL, FixMatch, FlexMatch, FreeMatch, SoftMatch, DebiasPL, V-PET, FineSSL) (my baseline above) to TriNoL, predict the resulting value for each: CIFAR-100 N4 (Labeled Only) accuracy (in %); CIFAR-100 N25 (Labeled Only) accuracy (in %); CIFAR-100 N100 (Labeled Only) accuracy (in %); FOOD-101 N2 (Labeled Only) accuracy (in %); FOOD-101 N4 (Labeled Only) accuracy (in %); FOOD-101 N10 (Labeled Only) accuracy (in %); Semi-Aves D_in (FixMatch) accuracy (in %); Semi-Aves D_in+D_out (FixMatch) accuracy (in %); ImageNet 1% (FixMatch) accuracy (in %); ImageNet 10% (FixMatch) accuracy (in %).

title: Triple Expert Learning from Noisy Labels for Semi-Supervised Vision Foundation Model Adaptation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how to handle semi-supervised adaptation of a frozen vision foundation model backbone when using confidence routing over three LoRA experts plus classifier head fine-tuning. The backbone parameters, denoted by $\psi$, stay frozen, and a lightweight LoRA module is inserted into selected linear projections; only the LoRA experts and the classifier head are trainable.

The idea I want to test is whether giving each confidence region its own expert-specific objective matters, versus just routing samples by confidence but training all experts with the same shared hard pseudo-label (CE) loss. In the shared CE setup, confidence routing determines which expert handles which samples, but every expert is optimized with the same hard pseudo-label loss regardless of its assigned confidence region. This contrasts with the variant where the Positive Expert on high-confidence samples uses $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pos}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{u}^{+}|} \sum_{u_i\in \mathcal{B}_{u}^{+}} \operatorname{CE}(\operatorname{softmax}(z^{+}(u_i^s)), \hat{y}_i)$, the Alignment Expert on medium-confidence samples uses $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{u}^{a}|} \sum_{u_i\in \mathcal{B}_{u}^{a}} \operatorname{KL}(\operatorname{sg}(p_i^w) \,\Vert\, \operatorname{softmax}(z^{a}(u_i^s)))$ (with $\operatorname{sg}(\cdot)$ the stop-gradient and $\operatorname{KL}(\cdot\Vert\cdot)$ the Kullback-Leibler divergence), and the Negative Expert on low-confidence samples uses $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neg}} = -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{u}^{-}|} \sum_{u_i\in \mathcal{B}_{u}^{-}} \log(1 - p_{i,\hat{y}_i}^{-} + \epsilon)$, where $p_i^{-}=\operatorname{softmax}(z^{-}(u_i^s))$, $p_{i,\hat{y}_i}^{-}$ is the probability the Negative Expert assigns to the weak-view top pseudo-label, and $\epsilon$ is a small constant for numerical stability. The full objective combines these with the supervised loss as $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{pos}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pos}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{neg}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neg}}$, where $\lambda_{\mathrm{pos}}$, $\lambda_{\mathrm{align}}$, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{neg}}$ control the strength of each term; in practice $\lambda_{\mathrm{pos}}$ is usually set larger since high-confidence pseudo-labels give the most direct supervision, the alignment weight controls how much medium-confidence samples influence the decision boundary, and the negative weight is kept moderate so as not to over-penalize uncertain samples.

The motivation is that routing samples by confidence is useful on its own, but I want to test whether each confidence region additionally needs a learning objective suited to its reliability level -- reliable, ambiguous, and unreliable pseudo-labels routed to different adaptation pathways with expert-specific losses, rather than all pathways sharing one hard pseudo-label loss.

My current setup compares Confidence Routing + Shared CE (all experts trained with the same hard pseudo-label loss under confidence routing) against the full TriNoL routing with expert-specific objectives, across several representative settings, including some with OOD unlabeled data (FOOD-101 N2 and Semi-Aves).

My baseline results for Confidence Routing + Shared CE are: CIFAR-100 N4 accuracy = 80.69%, FOOD-101 N2 accuracy = 87.84%, Semi-Aves accuracy = 61.47%, and ImageNet 1% accuracy = 74.55%.

My question about this setup: after switching from Confidence Routing + Shared CE (my baseline above) to TriNoL Routing, predict the resulting value for each: CIFAR-100 N4 accuracy (in %); FOOD-101 N2 accuracy (in %); Semi-Aves accuracy (in %); ImageNet 1% accuracy (in %).

title: Privileged Solutions or Context-Induced Teacher Behavior? Dissecting On-Policy Self-Distillation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming a variant of on-policy self-distillation to test whether the instance-level alignment between a target problem and its privileged teacher-only reference is actually necessary for the gains seen with the paired-target setup (which I'll call OPSD, using targetopsd notation). In OPSD, the teacher is given the reference solution paired with the current target problem during training. The variant I'm setting up, OP2SD, keeps the same on-policy training procedure but replaces that paired reference with a problem-and-solution pair drawn from a different training instance -- a 'worked example.' Formally, for each target problem x_i, I select another problem x_j and its reference solution y_j^\star (with j \neq i), and the teacher conditions on both the target problem and this worked example: p_T^{\mathrm{other}}(\cdot\mid x_i,x_j,y_j^\star) = p_0(\cdot\mid x_i,x_j,y_j^\star). The student policy itself is unchanged, the teacher does not generate a separate response, and the paired target solution y_i^\star is never included in the conditioning context of either policy. The teacher's prompt explicitly identifies (x_j,y_j^\star) as a worked example from a different problem and states it should not be treated as a solution or hint for the target problem.

Both the OPSD and OP2SD conditions share the same rollout construction and token-level distillation objective. Using m \in \{\mathrm{target},\mathrm{other}\}, with c_i^{\mathrm{target}}=y_i^\star and c_i^{\mathrm{other}}=(x_j,y_j^\star), the current student first samples a response, and student and teacher then evaluate the same student-generated prefixes. The objective is:
\mathcal L_m(\theta) = \mathbb E_{(x_i,y_i^\star)\sim\mathcal D} \mathbb E_{\hat y_i\sim p_S(\cdot\mid x_i)} \left[ \frac{1}{|\hat y_i|} \sum_{t=1}^{|\hat y_i|} D\!\left( p_T^m(\cdot\mid x_i,c_i^m,\hat y_{i,<t}) \,\middle\|\, p_S(\cdot\mid x_i,\hat y_{i,<t}) \right) \right].
D is the token-level divergence between teacher and student next-token distributions, and in my experiments both conditions use the same clipped Forward-KL surrogate, with the teacher distribution treated as a fixed target so gradients propagate only through the student. The two conditions differ only in the teacher-only context c_i^m: OPSD uses the reference paired with the target, while OP2SD uses the worked example from another problem. Everything else -- student input, rollout construction, teacher model, distillation objective, optimization procedure -- stays the same.

My setup evaluates this using Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B as students. For Qwen3-1.7B, the student p_S is non-thinking while the teacher p_T is thinking; for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, both student p_S and teacher p_T are non-thinking. All main experiments run on the OpenThoughts Math dataset (siyanzhao/Openthoughts_math_30k_opsd), following the existing OPSD experimental setup. For each model setting, I compare OP2SD against OPSD and against the base model. In OP2SD, each target problem is paired with a worked example drawn from the same training dataset; the worked-example pool consists of entries labeled amc_aime or aops_forum that exclude AIME2024, AIME2025, and HMMT Feb 2025 from the OpenThoughts Math dataset, with each selected example including both a problem and its reference solution. Evaluation is on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025, generating 12 outputs under each of four different seeds per problem.

My current baseline results, all under the OPSD (targetopsd) condition, are as follows. For Qwen3-1.7B: AIME 2024 Avg@12 = 55.42%, Pass@12 = 78.33%; AIME 2025 Avg@12 = 40.35%, Pass@12 = 65.0%; HMMT 2025 Avg@12 = 25.76%, Pass@12 = 50.83%. For Qwen3-4B: AIME 2024 Avg@12 = 30.76%, Pass@12 = 59.17%; AIME 2025 Avg@12 = 23.06%, Pass@12 = 50.0%; HMMT 2025 Avg@12 = 15.42%, Pass@12 = 35.83%. title: Privileged Solutions or Context-Induced Teacher Behavior? Dissecting On-Policy Self-Distillation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming a variant of OPSD, which I'm calling OP2SD, that keeps the same on-policy training procedure but changes the source of the teacher-only reference context. In OPSD, the teacher receives the reference solution paired with the current target problem. In OP2SD, that paired reference is instead replaced by a problem and solution pair drawn from a different training instance (a "worked example"). The idea is to test whether instance-level alignment between the target problem and the privileged reference is actually necessary for the OPSD gain.

Formally, for each target problem \(x_i\), I select another problem \(x_j\) and its reference solution \(y_j^\star\), with \(j\neq i\), and call the pair \((x_j,y_j^\star)\) the worked-example. The student policy is unchanged, but the teacher now conditions on both the target problem and the worked-example:
\begin{equation}
 p_T^{\mathrm{other}}(\cdot\mid x_i,x_j,y_j^\star)
 =
 p_0(\cdot\mid x_i,x_j,y_j^\star).
 \label{eq:other-problem-policy}
\end{equation}
As in target-solution OPSD, the teacher doesn't generate a separate response, and the paired target solution \(y_i^\star\) is never included in the conditioning context of either policy. The teacher's prompt explicitly identifies \((x_j,y_j^\star)\) as a worked example from a different problem and states that it should not be treated as a solution or hint.

My setup uses Qwen3-4B, with both the student and teacher in non-thinking mode during training. All main experiments run on the OpenThoughts Math dataset (siyanzhao/Openthoughts_math_30k_opsd). In OP2SD, each target problem is paired with a worked-example drawn from the same training dataset; the worked-example pool consists of entries labeled amc_aime or aops_forum that exclude AIME2024, AIME2025, and HMMT Feb 2025, and each selected example includes both a problem and its reference solution. I evaluate on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025, generating 12 outputs under each of four different seeds per problem.

For this particular comparison, I'm evaluating the Qwen3-4B model trained in non-thinking mode (with either OPSD or OP2SD) at inference time with thinking enabled, without any further training, to see whether the training-time behavior transfers across inference modes.

My current baseline results for OPSD under this thinking-mode evaluation are: on AIME 2024, Avg@12 = 70.9%, Pass@12 = 85.0%, Vote@12 = 80.83%; on AIME 2025, Avg@12 = 64.03%, Pass@12 = 82.5%, Vote@12 = 76.67%; and on HMMT 2025, Avg@12 = 44.44%, Pass@12 = 68.33%, Vote@12 = 55.83%.

My question about this setup: after switching from OPSD (my baseline above) to OP2SD, predict the resulting value for each: AIME 2024 Avg@12 (in %); AIME 2024 Pass@12 (in %); AIME 2024 Vote@12 (in %); AIME 2025 Avg@12 (in %); AIME 2025 Pass@12 (in %); AIME 2025 Vote@12 (in %); HMMT 2025 Avg@12 (in %); HMMT 2025 Pass@12 (in %); HMMT 2025 Vote@12 (in %).

title: Privileged Solutions or Context-Induced Teacher Behavior? Dissecting On-Policy Self-Distillation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about what actually drives the gains in OPSD (on-policy self-distillation with privileged information). The standard account, which lines up with the broader learning-using-privileged-information literature, is that the teacher's access to privileged information about the current problem is what matters: the teacher gets the verified (partial) answer and reasoning trace for the same problem the student is solving (the "reference solution" or "target solution"), and the student learns from the teacher's predictions conditioned on that target-specific information.

But I think providing a reference solution changes more than just what the teacher knows about the target — it also changes the context under which the teacher produces token-level supervision. A worked solution can alter the teacher's next-token distribution through its reasoning structure, notation, style, and effects on continuation/termination, even if it carries no information about the current instance at all. So I want to separate target-specific privilege from context-induced teacher behavior. The central question I'm probing is whether OPSD actually requires privileged information about the current target, or whether a teacher-only worked-solution context — even one unrelated to the current problem — can induce a useful supervisory distribution.

To test this, my setup (OP2SD) retains the on-policy training procedure of OPSD but changes the source of the teacher-only reference context. In OPSD, the teacher receives the reference solution paired with the current target. In OP2SD, that paired reference is replaced by a problem-and-solution pair from a different training instance. This is designed to test whether instance-level alignment between the target problem and the privileged reference is actually necessary for the OPSD gain.

The worked-problem domain control uses a deterministic split of Omni-MATH, which doesn't provide an official train/test split for this experiment. I select 1,280 Algebra-tagged, non-Geometry training targets and 30 disjoint held-out targets, balanced across lower, middle, and upper annotated difficulty. Each OP2SD arm uses a 320-example worked-example pool: Algebra/non-Geometry for the in-domain arm and Geometry-only for the out-of-domain arm. The worked examples share source provenance and are aligned by difficulty and Qwen-tokenized context length; both arms use the same deterministic target-to-context-example index mapping.

I'm training Qwen3-1.7B with training seed 42, 100 updates, and an effective batch of 32 (plus the rest of my usual optimization settings). This gives 3,200 target exposures, or 2.5 passes over the target set. I evaluate checkpoint 100 with 12 samples per problem and 4 seeds, on the held-out Omni-MATH Algebra split.

My current baseline, using OPSD (current target solution), on this held-out Omni-MATH Algebra split is: Avg@12 = 66.74%, Pass@12 = 76.67%, Vote@12 = 70.0%. (Restating: Avg@12 = 66.74%, Pass@12 = 76.67%, Vote@12 = 70.0%.)

It's on-policy because supervision is provided on prefixes generated by the current student, and it's self-distillation because the student and teacher come from the same model rather than models of different sizes.

 p_S(\cdot\mid x_i)
 =p_\theta(\cdot\mid x_i), \qquad
 p_T^{\mathrm{target}}(\cdot\mid x_i,y_i^\star)
 =p_0(\cdot\mid x_i,y_i^\star).
 \label{eq:clean-policies}
\end{equation}
The teacher does not generate an alternative solution, so its advantage does not derive from a larger parameter count but from its privileged access to $y_i^\star$.

When the teacher is given a worked reference solution for the current target problem, this changes not just what the teacher knows about that specific target, but also the context under which it produces its token-level supervision. A worked solution could alter the teacher's next-token distribution through its reasoning structure, notation, style, and its effects on continuation and termination, even if it conveys no direct information about the current instance. My central question is whether OPSD's gain requires privileged information about the current target, or whether a teacher-only worked-solution context can induce a useful supervisory distribution without revealing the actual target's solution.

To test this, I set up OP2SD as a variant where the paired reference is replaced by a problem and solution pair drawn from a different training instance, rather than the target's own paired reference. This intervention is meant to test whether instance-level alignment between the target problem and the privileged reference is actually necessary for the OPSD gain.

My experimental setup: I'm using Qwen3-4B with a matched non-thinking student and non-thinking teacher (as part of a broader set that also includes Qwen3-1.7B with non-thinking student/thinking teacher, and Qwen3-8B with non-thinking student/teacher). All main experiments are conducted on the OpenThoughts Math dataset (siyanzhao/Openthoughts_math_30k_opsd), following the established experimental setup for OPSD. For each model setting, I compare my method against OPSD (targetopsd) and the base model. In my method, each target problem is paired with a worked example drawn from the same training dataset; the worked-example pool consists of entries labeled amc_aime or aops_forum that exclude AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025 problems from the OpenThoughts Math dataset, and each selected example includes both a problem and its reference solution. I evaluate on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025. For each problem, I generate 12 outputs under each of four different seeds.

My current baseline, using OPSD with the paired (target-matched) reference solution on Qwen3-4B, gives: on AIME 2024, Avg@12 = 30.76%, Pass@12 = 59.17%, Vote@12 = 45.83%; on AIME 2025, Avg@12 = 23.06%, Pass@12 = 50.0%, Vote@12 = 28.33%; on HMMT 2025, Avg@12 = 15.42%, Pass@12 = 35.83%, Vote@12 = 20.83%.

title: Privileged Solutions or Context-Induced Teacher Behavior? Dissecting On-Policy Self-Distillation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how to isolate what actually drives the gains in OPSD-style training, where a student is trained on-policy against a teacher that has access to a paired reference (problem + solution) for the same target instance. The standard explanation, consistent with the broader literature on learning using privileged information, is that the teacher's gain comes from its access to target-specific privileged information: the teacher sees the verified reference solution for the current problem, and the student learns from the teacher's predictions conditioned on that target-specific context. But I've been thinking that providing a reference solution changes not just what the teacher knows about the target, but also the context under which it produces token-level supervision — a worked solution can alter the teacher's next-token distribution through its reasoning structure, notation, style, and effects on continuation/termination, even if it conveys no information about the current instance. So I want to distinguish target-specific privilege from context-induced teacher behavior.

To test this, I set up a variant I'm calling OP2SD, which retains the same on-policy training procedure as OPSD (\targetopsd) but changes the source of the teacher-only reference context. In OPSD, the teacher receives the reference solution paired with the current target problem. In OP2SD, that paired reference is instead replaced by a problem-and-solution pair drawn from a different training instance. The idea is to test whether instance-level alignment between the target problem and the privileged reference is actually necessary for the OPSD gain, or whether context-induced effects alone could account for some of it.

My setup uses Qwen3-8B, with both the student and teacher in non-thinking mode (matched configuration), trained on the OpenThoughts Math dataset (siyanzhao/Openthoughts_math_30k_opsd), following the same experimental setup as the OPSD reference work. For each target problem in OP2SD, I pair it with a worked example drawn from the same training dataset; the worked-example pool consists of entries labeled amc_aime or aops_forum that exclude AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025, and each selected example includes both a problem and its reference solution.

The training configuration shared by OPSD and OP2SD for Qwen3-8B non-thinking is: base model Qwen3-8B; training dataset siyanzhao/Openthoughts_math_30k_opsd; training seed 42; per-device batch size / gradient accumulation = 2 / 4; student and teacher mode both non-thinking; maximum student completion 1,024 tokens; student sampling at temperature 1.1, top-p 0.95, top-k 20; learning rate 5×10^-6, constant; maximum gradient norm 0.1; LoRA adapter with r=64, alpha=128; teacher is a frozen base model with LoRA disabled; objective is forward KL at temperature 1.1 with beta=0; KL clip tau=10^-7.

I evaluate on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025, generating 12 outputs per problem under each of four different seeds, and I report Avg@12, Pass@12, and Vote@12.

My current baseline, using OPSD (\targetopsd) on this Qwen3-8B non-thinking setup, gets: on AIME 2024, Avg@12 = 45.0 points, Pass@12 = 74.17 points, Vote@12 = 61.67 points; on AIME 2025, Avg@12 = 32.15 points, Pass@12 = 58.33 points, Vote@12 = 40.0 points; and on HMMT Feb 2025, Avg@12 = 16.18 points, Pass@12 = 39.17 points, Vote@12 = 20.0 points.

title: Privileged Solutions or Context-Induced Teacher Behavior? Dissecting On-Policy Self-Distillation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about a way to test whether the on-policy self-distillation gains from OPSD actually depend on the teacher seeing a reference solution that's paired to the exact target problem, or whether just having some worked example in context is enough. The idea, which I'm calling OP2SD (self-distillation from other problems), keeps the same on-policy training procedure as OPSD but swaps out the teacher-only reference context: instead of the teacher conditioning on the target problem's own paired reference solution, it conditions on a problem and solution pair drawn from a different training instance. Formally, for each target problem x_i, I select another problem x_j and its reference solution y_j^\star (with j\neq i), calling the pair (x_j,y_j^\star) the worked-example. The student policy is unchanged, while the teacher instead conditions on both the target problem and the worked-example: p_T^{\mathrm{other}}(\cdot\mid x_i,x_j,y_j^\star) = p_0(\cdot\mid x_i,x_j,y_j^\star). As in the target solution OPSD, the teacher does not generate a separate response, and the paired target solution y_i^\star is not included in the conditioning context of either policy. The teacher's prompt explicitly identifies (x_j,y_j^\star) as a worked example from a different problem and states that it should not be treated as a solution or hint for x_i. This is meant to test whether instance-level alignment between the target problem and the privileged reference is necessary for the OPSD gain.

My setup uses Qwen3-1.7B, with the student non-thinking and the teacher thinking, trained on the OpenThoughts Math dataset (siyanzhao/Openthoughts_math_30k_opsd), following the same experimental setup as the original OPSD work. I compare OP2SD against OPSD and the base model (Base). In OP2SD, each target problem is paired with a worked-example drawn from the same training dataset; the worked-example pool consists of entries labeled amc_aime or aops_forum that do not include AIME2024, AIME2025, or HMMT Feb 2025 in the OpenThoughts Math dataset, and each selected example includes both a problem and its reference solution. I evaluate on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT Feb 2025, generating 12 outputs under each of four different seeds per problem.

As part of this, I'm looking at problem-by-problem performance to understand whether aggregate Avg@12 gains come from solving problems Base never solves or from increasing the probability of correct answers on problems Base already solves occasionally. For Qwen3-1.7B, pooling results across the four seeds, for each problem i and method m, c_i^{(m)} in {0,...,48} denotes the number of correct responses among 12 samples under each of four seeds, and I compute the Pearson correlation between problem-level correct counts for every pair of methods, along with how often one method has a higher, equal, or lower count than another across all 90 benchmark problems.

My baseline results for the Pearson correlation of problem-level correct counts between OPSD and Base, pooled across the four training seeds, are: on AIME24, 0.942r; on AIME25, 0.974r; on HMMT25, 0.974r; and pooled across all three (All), 0.966r.

My question about this setup: after switching from OPSD vs. Base (my baseline above) to OP2SD vs. Base, predict the resulting value for each: AIME24 Pearson correlation of problem-level correct counts (in r); AIME25 Pearson correlation of problem-level correct counts (in r); HMMT25 Pearson correlation of problem-level correct counts (in r); All (pooled) Pearson correlation of problem-level correct counts (in r).

I've been brainstorming an attack pipeline against Claude Opus 4.6 that targets stereotype-related harms, evaluated on a stratified sample of the BBQ stereotype benchmark. One step in this attack is a Turn 2 step that performs presupposition inference, which recovers the background assumption supporting an identified stereotype rather than stating it outright. For instance, in one case the model is led to infer the presupposition that "people from other countries are inherently dangerous enemies." The idea is that this presupposition step induces the model to infer an implicit context in which the harmful request becomes relevant, using pragmatic inference to construct that unstated context.

To isolate the contribution of this presupposition/pragmatic-inference step, my setup is an ablation study on Claude Opus where I replace the presupposition turn with an explicit request to describe situations in which the target stereotype applies. This variant preserves the same three-round interaction structure and the target topic, but removes the need for the model to infer the unstated context on its own — it's given the scenario explicitly instead.

My baseline result on the BBQ stereotype dataset, measured as Attack Success Rate, is: Full method (w/o presupposition) = 0.911 proportion.

title: Pragmatic Attack Surface: Vulnerabilities of Implicit Context in Large Language Models
prompt:
I've been brainstorming an attack method that infers the presuppositions underlying a harmful request to get at its implicit context, and then enriches that context to generate semantically diverse but pragmatically equivalent harmful outputs. I'm comparing this pragmatic (implicit-context) attack against an established multi-turn jailbreak baseline, ActorAttack, which first extracts the harmful target and selects an actor that supports an innocuous opening, then generates a question chain and rewrites a rejected turn up to two times before appending the canonical final objective. For context, I'm also adapting a second external baseline, Crescendo, which uses a stateful attacker that begins with an abstract request and progressively escalates by conditioning on the target's responses, backtracking and replacing a refused turn with a gentler alternative up to two times. For both of these external baselines (ActorAttack and Crescendo), I use DeepSeek-v4-Flash to generate the attack queries.

My evaluation setup covers four frontier LLM targets: GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 4.6, Qwen3.6-27B, and Gemini 3.6 Flash, chosen because they are among the most widely used and capable frontier models with advanced safety alignment. All main experiments run in the standard (non-extra-thinking) generation mode, though I additionally evaluate Claude Opus 4.6 in max thinking mode to check whether extended inference computing time affects the attack.

For measuring attack effectiveness I report two metrics. The first is Non-Refusal Rate, which checks whether the target model refuses to generate harmful outputs; for BBQ specifically, I extend the standard refusal-detection phrases with additions like 'without more information' and 'there is not enough', since lexical matching alone is insufficient because a model may refuse first while still providing harmful content later. The second metric is Attack Success Rate, where DeepSeek judges whether the output is harmful, following a benchmark-specific rubric that outputs exactly Yes or No: for BBQ, whether the response contains stereotypes or prejudicial generalizations; for Implicit Hate, whether it contains concrete hateful, threatening, or violence-inciting content; and for PolyGuard, whether it produces usable code or decision rules that unfairly rely on protected or other non-performance-related attributes. Responses rejected outright by the target model's built-in safety policy before any requested content is generated are also counted as unsuccessful attacks under Attack Success Rate. Since Non-Refusal Rate captures lexical refusal while Attack Success Rate captures semantic completion, these two metrics have different denominators and I report them separately rather than aggregating or averaging them.

For my ActorAttack baseline, evaluated against Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.6 Sol in standard generation mode with DeepSeek-v4-Flash generating the attack queries and DeepSeek judging attack success, my baseline results are as follows. On BBQ against Claude Opus 4.6: Non-Refusal Rate = 0.578, Attack Success Rate = 0.333. On BBQ against GPT-5.6 Sol: Non-Refusal Rate = 0.622, Attack Success Rate = 0.611. title: Adaptive Sequential Test Planning for Multi-Mechanism Reliability Qualification via Bayesian Monte Carlo Tree Search
prompt:
I've been brainstorming an adaptive test planning approach using MCTS-SA (Monte Carlo Tree Search for Seed-Action simulators) with progressive widening as the core planning mechanism, applied to a stochastic multi-mechanism reliability simulation environment covering BTI/EM/TDDB degradation. The idea is that MCTS builds a search tree through repeated simulations, each proceeding through four phases: (1) Selection, traversing the existing tree by treating child selection at each node as a multi-armed bandit problem, balancing exploitation of high-value branches with exploration of less-visited ones; (2) Expansion, adding a new node; (3) Rollout, simulating a complete test sequence from the new node using random decisions; and (4) Backpropagation, updating node statistics with the observed return. MCTS is an anytime algorithm with monotonically improving solution quality, naturally handles non-differentiable and discrete objectives, and under a seed-action formulation enables deterministic trajectory replay in stochastic environments.

My setup evaluates this adaptive test planning framework on the stochastic multi-mechanism environment (BTI/EM/TDDB), using a single calibrated device instance. Each planning run performs 5,000 iterations with a maximum test length of 300 epochs. The MCTS hyperparameters are: exploration constant C = 1.4, progressive widening k=3, alpha=0.5, and discount gamma = 1.0. I compare this against a 500-episode random policy baseline on the same device instance. Performance is assessed using metrics including Characterization yield (CY) — the fraction of test sequences achieving ΔV_t ≥ ΔV_fail without catastrophe, the primary measure of test planning effectiveness — and Catastrophe rate — the fraction of test sequences ending in EM or TDDB failure, the primary safety metric. Other tracked metrics include test length (number of epochs to termination) and final uncertainty (trace of posterior BTI parameter covariance).

My baseline results are: for the stochastic multi-mechanism reliability simulation (BTI/EM/TDDB), the random policy (500 episodes) achieves a Characterization yield (CY) of 16.0% and a Catastrophe rate of 84.0%.

title: EgoHieraLoc: A Cortically Inspired Hierarchical Segmentation-Guided Framework for Egocentric Visual Query Localization
prompt:
I've been brainstorming ways to extend the Geometric-Semantic Joint Confidence (GSJC) framework used in my EgoHieraLoc multi-view aggregation pipeline. The framework evaluates each candidate frame via four complementary factors: segmentation confidence, depth consistency, reprojection consistency, and triangulation baseline quality.

For depth consistency, my setup computes the within-mask depth variance for each frame as \begin{equation}\sigma_{d,i}^2 = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{SM}_i|}\sum_{(x,y)\in \mathcal{SM}_i}\left(\mathcal{D}_i(x,y) - \bar{\mathcal{D}}_i\right)^2.\end{equation} The depth consistency weight is then $\varpi_i^{\text{depth}} = \exp\left(-\frac{\sigma_{d,i}^2}{\sigma_0^2}\right)$, where $\sigma_0$ is the dataset median depth variance computed over validation frames, so frames with low within-mask variance get weights near 1 while high-variance regions are attenuated.

For triangulation quality, I define the optical ray direction in world coordinates by first computing the ray in camera coordinates and then rotating it back to world frame. Letting $\mathbf{r}_c = \mathcal{K}^{-1}[u_i, v_i, 1]^T$ be the unnormalized ray direction in camera space, the ray direction in world coordinates is \begin{equation}\mathbf{r}_i = \frac{R_i^T \mathbf{r}_c}{\parallel R_i^T \mathbf{r}_c \parallel_2},\end{equation} where $R_i$ is the rotation component of $\mathcal{T}_i$. The mean ray across all candidate frames is $\bar{\mathbf{r}} = \frac{1}{N_C}\sum_{j=1}^{N_C}\mathbf{r}_j$, and the baseline quality factor is $\varpi_i^{\text{tri}} = \sin(\theta_i) = \sqrt{1 - (\mathbf{r}_i \cdot \bar{\mathbf{r}})^2}$, where $\theta_i$ is the angle between ray $\mathbf{r}_i$ and the mean direction. To prevent numerical degeneracy when rays are nearly parallel, I clamp the result: $\varpi_i^{\text{tri}} = \max(\sin(\theta_i), 0.01)$. The idea here is that larger baseline angles should enhance triangulation stability, since orthogonal rays are less sensitive to depth noise.

All confidence factors are combined multiplicatively into a composite weight: \begin{equation}\tilde{\vartheta}_i = \max\left(\vartheta_i^{\text{sem}} \cdot \varpi_i^{\text{depth}} \cdot \varpi_i^{\text{reproj}} \cdot \varpi_i^{\text{tri}},\; \epsilon_w\right),\end{equation} where $\epsilon_w = 10^{-6}$ prevents numerical underflow. This multiplicative aggregation is meant to ensure that any significantly unreliable factor suppresses that frame's contribution, while frames robust across all dimensions receive full weight. The final 3D position is then computed as a confidence-weighted mean: \begin{equation}[\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z}]^T = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N_C} \tilde{\vartheta}_j \cdot [x_j, y_j, z_j]^T}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_C} \tilde{\vartheta}_j}.\end{equation} When all frames are severely unreliable and all weights clamp to $\epsilon_w$, the denominator approaches $N_C \epsilon_w$ and the aggregation defaults to an unweighted average, which is intended to keep things numerically stable.

My current experimental setup is an ablation on the EgoHieraLoc GSJC multi-view aggregation module, evaluated on the Ego4D-VQ3D validation set, where I'm looking specifically at the effect of adding these geometric reliability factors ($\varpi^{\text{depth}}$ and $\varpi^{\text{tri}}$) on top of a semantic-only baseline. My baseline configuration uses all three semantic checks with no geometric weights applied, and on Ego4D-VQ3D it gets Succ = 81.42%, Succ* = 96.93%, and L2 error = 1.37m.

My question about this setup: after switching from Semantic-only (all three semantic checks, no geometric weights) (my baseline above) to + Partial Geometric Weights (varpi^depth, varpi^reproj, varpi^tri individually), predict the resulting value for each: Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^depth weight Succ (in %); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^depth weight Succ* (in %); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^depth weight L2 error (in m); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^reproj weight Succ (in %); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^reproj weight Succ* (in %); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^reproj weight L2 error (in m); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^tri weight Succ (in %); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^tri weight Succ* (in %); Ego4D-VQ3D, varpi^tri weight L2 error (in m).

The setup works by triangulating N_C candidate frames, back-projecting each into 3D points {x_j, y_j, z_j}_{j=1}^{N_C}, and computing their mean p̄ = (1/N_C) Σ_{j=1}^{N_C} [x_j, y_j, z_j]^T. This consensus point is then reprojected back to frame i by transforming to camera coordinates and projecting: p̄_c = T_i [p̄; 1], [û_i, v̂_i]^T = K · p̄_c^{(1:2)} / p̄_c^{(3)}, where p̄_c^{(1:2)} and p̄_c^{(3)} denote the xy and z components of the camera-frame point. From this I derive a reprojection weight varpi_i^{reproj} = exp(-‖[u_i,v_i]^T - [û_i,v̂_i]^T‖_2 / ε_r), where the tolerance is scaled by object size: ε_r = max(10, 0.02 × bbox_diag). This adaptive tolerance is typically 10--25 pixels for egocentric objects, meant to give scale-dependent consistency checking so that frames whose back-projected consensus aligns well with the original 2D observation receive higher weights.

More broadly, all confidence factors are combined multiplicatively into a composite weight: ϑ̃_i = max(ϑ_i^{sem} · varpi_i^{depth} · varpi_i^{reproj} · varpi_i^{tri}, ε_w), with ε_w = 10^{-6} to prevent numerical underflow. The final 3D position is then computed as a confidence-weighted mean: [x̂, ŷ, ẑ]^T = Σ_{j=1}^{N_C} ϑ̃_j · [x_j, y_j, z_j]^T / Σ_{j=1}^{N_C} ϑ̃_j. If all frames are severely unreliable and all weights clamp to ε_w, the denominator approaches N_C·ε_w and the aggregation defaults to an unweighted average, which is intended to keep things numerically stable.

prompt:
I've been brainstorming ways to make the multi-view aggregation step in my 3D displacement estimation pipeline more robust by combining semantic and geometric cues into a single confidence score. The overall framework I'm calling GSJC (Geometric-Semantic Joint Confidence) evaluates each candidate frame using four complementary factors: segmentation confidence, depth consistency, reprojection consistency, and triangulation baseline quality. The idea I want to test now is adding the triangulation baseline geometric weight, $\varpi_i^{\text{tri}}$, on top of the full semantic GSJC formulation.

For the triangulation baseline factor, my setup defines the optical ray direction in world coordinates by first computing the ray in camera coordinates and then rotating it back to the world frame. I let $\mathbf{r}_c = \mathcal{K}^{-1}[u_i, v_i, 1]^T$ denote the unnormalized ray direction in camera space, and the ray direction in world coordinates is $\mathbf{r}_i = \frac{R_i^T \mathbf{r}_c}{\parallel R_i^T \mathbf{r}_c \parallel_2}$, where $R_i$ is the rotation component of $\mathcal{T}_i$. The mean ray across all candidate frames is $\bar{\mathbf{r}} = \frac{1}{N_C}\sum_{j=1}^{N_C}\mathbf{r}_j$. The baseline quality factor is $\varpi_i^{\text{tri}} = \sin(\theta_i) = \sqrt{1 - (\mathbf{r}_i \cdot \bar{\mathbf{r}})^2}$, where $\theta_i$ is the angle between ray $\mathbf{r}_i$ and the mean direction. To prevent numerical degeneracy when rays are nearly parallel, I clamp the result: $\varpi_i^{\text{tri}} = \max(\sin(\theta_i), 0.01)$. The motivation is that larger baseline angles should enhance triangulation stability, since orthogonal rays are less sensitive to depth noise.

All confidence factors are combined multiplicatively into a composite weight: $\tilde{\vartheta}_i = \max\left(\vartheta_i^{\text{sem}} \cdot \varpi_i^{\text{depth}} \cdot \varpi_i^{\text{reproj}} \cdot \varpi_i^{\text{tri}},\; \epsilon_w\right)$, where $\epsilon_w = 10^{-6}$ prevents numerical underflow. This multiplicative aggregation is meant to ensure that any significantly unreliable factor suppresses that frame's contribution, while frames robust across all dimensions get full weight. The final 3D position is computed as a confidence-weighted mean: $[\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z}]^T = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N_C} \tilde{\vartheta}_j \cdot [x_j, y_j, z_j]^T}{\sum_{j=1}^{N_C} \tilde{\vartheta}_j}$. Finally, I transform the aggregated world position into the query frame's coordinate system via the inverse query pose: $\boldsymbol{\delta} = \mathcal{T}_{\text{query}}^{-1}[\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z}, 1]^T$, which yields the VQL-3D prediction.

title: Matryoshka Language Model Suites
prompt:
I've been iterating on how the inter-model junction in a Matryoshka suite interacts with distillation, and I set up an ablation to isolate it. Since every forward pass through the full model \theta_M already produces logits for all M sub-models simultaneously, online distillation from the largest sub-model to all smaller ones comes essentially for free, so I'm exploring how much of the recipe's performance depends on that signal versus on the junction design itself (with and without the norm-rescaling and the fresh embedding at the junction) and on how layers are allocated across sub-models. Concretely, I add a distillation term to each sub-model m < M defined as the cross-entropy between the teacher and student next-token distributions: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}^{M \to m}_d = - \sum_{v=1}^{V} \texttt{stop\_grad}(\sigma(l^M_t)_v) \, \log \sigma(l^m_t)_v, \label{eq:distillation} \end{equation} where \sigma denotes the softmax. The total loss for sub-model m is a convex combination: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}^m = (1 - \alpha_d)\,\mathcal{L}^m_{\mathrm{ce}} + \alpha_d\,\mathcal{L}^{M \to m}_d, \label{eq:submodel-loss} \end{equation} and the overall training objective sums over sub-models: \mathcal{L} = \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{L}^m, with \alpha_d \in [0,1] controlling the strength of the teacher signal. The total loss for sub-model $m$ is a convex combination: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}^m = (1 - \alpha_d)\,\mathcal{L}^m_{\mathrm{ce}} + \alpha_d\,\mathcal{L}^{M \to m}_d, \label{eq:submodel-loss} \end{equation} and the overall training objective sums over sub-models: $\mathcal{L} = \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{L}^m$. title: MarkNull: Model-Agnostic Watermark Removal in AI-Generated Images via On-Manifold Latent Manipulation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming an attack against AI-generated image watermarking that operates in a strict no-box setting, relying only on a proxy diffusion model rather than the actual watermarking model or its outputs. The core idea is to measure and then break the correlation between the initial latent $z_0$ (the VAE-encoded latent of the watermarked image) and the sampled noise $z_T$ that the diffusion model would map it toward. I introduce a metric NLAS to quantify this correlation: \begin{equation}\mathrm{NLAS}(z_0,z_T) = ( \arccos\left( \frac{z_0 \cdot z_T}{\|z_0\|_2 \|z_T\|_2} \right) - \frac{\pi}{2} )^2.\end{equation} The idea is that $z_0$ shows high alignment with its coupled $z_T$, while it is effectively orthogonal to a random standard Gaussian noise $z_{\text{rand}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$. Building on this, I want to construct an adversarial latent $z_0^{(\mathrm{adv})}$ that is pushed toward orthogonality with $z_T$: \begin{equation}\begin{aligned} &\theta(z_0^{(\mathrm{adv})}, z_T) \to \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \left| \langle \frac{z_0^{(\mathrm{adv})}}{\|z_0^{(\mathrm{adv})}\|}, \frac{z_T}{\|z_T\|} \rangle \right| \approx 0,\\ \end{aligned}\end{equation} where $\langle \cdot,\cdot \rangle$ denotes the inner product, enforcing statistical independence under a Gaussian prior. To preserve visual fidelity while optimizing $z_0^{(\mathrm{adv})}$, I add an image quality loss constraining the decoded adversarial image to stay close to the original watermarked image: \begin{equation}\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{img}}(I_A, I_w) &= \lambda_1\,\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{LPIPS}(I_A, I_w) + \lambda_2\,\|I_A - I_w\|_2^2\\ &+ \lambda_3\,\big(1-\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{SSIM}(I_A, I_w)\big), \end{aligned}\end{equation} where $I_w$ and $I_A$ are the original watermarked image and the image decoded from the adversarial latent via the proxy model, respectively; $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{LPIPS}$ measures perceptual dissimilarity, $\|\cdot\|_2^2$ is pixel-wise MSE, and $\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{SSIM}$ quantifies structural similarity, with $\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3\}$ balancing the three terms. I aggregate all these terms into a unified objective and optimize $z_0^{(\mathrm{adv})}$ via gradient descent, using only the proxy model $\Theta^A=(\mathcal{E}^A, \mathcal{U}^A,\mathcal{D}^A)$ to stay strictly within the no-box setting. I call this per-instance attack MarkNull. Separately, I'm also exploring an amortized variant, MarkNull-A, designed to improve attack efficiency: instead of iterative per-sample optimization, MarkNull-A employs a WRN (watermark removal network) trained to learn a direct mapping from watermarked images to their watermark-free counterparts via a single feed-forward pass, minimizing an analogous objective function, rather than optimizing each sample from scratch. For my experimental setup, I deploy nine representative AI-generated image watermarking baselines spanning three paradigms: post-hoc watermarking (DWT-DCT-SVD / DwtDct, RivaGan, HiDDeN), fine-tuning-based watermarking (Stable Signature / SS, VINE, SleeperMark), and initial-noise-based watermarking (Gaussian Shading / GS, PRC, TreeRing / TR). TR is a zero-bit watermarking scheme verified without decoding, while the others are multi-bit. I use Stable Diffusion 2.1-base (SD2.1) as the default backbone for both image generation and watermark embedding, sampling prompts from the Stable Diffusion Prompts (SDP) dataset and generating 100 watermarked images at 512×512 resolution per watermarking method, with a fixed 50 inference steps. For the post-hoc baselines specifically, I instead generate 100 images using Stable Diffusion XL-base 1.0 (SDXL1.0) and apply the watermarking schemes afterward. When a proxy model is needed by the adversary, I instantiate it using Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5). For evaluation, I look at watermark removal effectiveness by measuring detection scores: for multi-bit schemes I report BA (bit accuracy), and for the zero-bit TR scheme I report TPR@1%FPR. My current baseline results with MarkNull (no attack-free detection is near-perfect for all schemes) are: DwtDct BA = 55.1%, RivaGan BA = 59.78%, HiDDeN BA = 60.62%, SS BA = 49.12%, VINE BA = 64.93%, SleeperMark BA = 42.88%, GS BA = 41.55%, PRC BA = 51.18%, and TR TPR@1%FPR = 43.0%.

My question about this setup: after switching from MarkNull (my baseline above) to MarkNull-A, predict the resulting value for each: DwtDct BA (in %); RivaGan BA (in %); HiDDeN BA (in %); SS BA (in %); VINE BA (in %); SleeperMark BA (in %); GS BA (in %); PRC BA (in %); TR TPR@1%FPR (in %).

title: MarkNull: Model-Agnostic Watermark Removal in AI-Generated Images via On-Manifold Latent Manipulation
prompt:
I've been brainstorming ways to evaluate watermark-removal attacks in a way that captures overall image quality rather than any single metric, and I've been building on an amortized attack idea that grows out of a per-instance optimization approach. The starting observation is that a powerful per-instance attack relies on iterative gradient-based optimization, which is computationally costly and limits scalability, but the perturbations it learns turn out to have consistent, transferable structural patterns across samples. That suggests the transformation needed to decorrelate watermark signals from the latent diffusion trajectory is learnable and generalizable, which motivated an amortized variant (MarkNull-A) that replaces iterative per-sample optimization with a single feed-forward model (a WRN) to amortize the optimization cost through one forward pass.

To assess image quality in a holistic way, I'm using a composite quality score (CQS) that aggregates PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and BRISQUE into one unified score. It's computed as CQS = sum over metrics m of S_m, where for PSNR and SSIM, S_m = (v_m - v_m^min) / (v_m^max - v_m^min), and for LPIPS, FID, and BRISQUE, S_m = (v_m^max - v_m) / (v_m^max - v_m^min), with v_m being the value of metric m and v_m^min, v_m^max being its min/max across the compared methods.
